title: Dot products, angles, and projections
objective: Calculate dot products, classify and measure angles between nonzero vectors, and distinguish scalar components, vector projections, and work along a displacement.
why: The dot product measures alignment and connects geometry to useful calculations such as projection and work. Recovering its scalar meaning helps you distinguish a component along a direction from the vector that carries that component.

prerequisites.label: Vector arithmetic, resultants, and coordinate directions

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: For matching Cartesian components, $u\cdot v=u_xv_x+u_yv_y+u_zv_z$. The result is one scalar. For nonzero vectors it also equals $\|u\|\|v\|\cos\theta$, where 0≤θ≤180° is the angle between them.
Projection of u onto nonzero v is $\operatorname{proj}_v u=(u\cdot v)/(v\cdot v)\,v$. The signed scalar component along v is $(u\cdot v)/\|v\|$. Keep these scalar and vector answers distinct.

sections.heading: Multiply matching components, then sum
paragraphs: The dot symbol represents a specific operation. Multiplying two component lists coordinate by coordinate gives intermediate products, but those products must then be added. In an orthonormal frame, the basis dot products are i·i=1 and i·j=0, explaining why matching coordinates survive and mixed directions disappear.

The dot product is symmetric: u·v=v·u. It distributes across addition, so u·(v+w)=u·v+u·w. These properties support projection checks, but they do not carry over unchanged to the cross product in the next lesson. Identify the operation before applying a familiar rule.

sections.heading: The sign tells you about alignment
paragraphs: For two nonzero vectors, the magnitudes in the angle formula are positive. The dot-product sign therefore follows the cosine sign: positive for an acute angle, zero for a right angle, and negative for an obtuse angle. The angle between opposite nonzero vectors is 180°, not a negative angle.

Divide the dot product by the product of magnitudes before taking inverse cosine. The exact ratio lies between -1 and 1. A calculator may create a tiny rounding excursion at an endpoint; keep enough precision and check the exact geometry. If either vector is zero, the angle formula divides by zero. A zero dot product alone does not establish a geometric right angle in that case.

sections.heading: A projection separates along from perpendicular
paragraphs: The vector projection lies on the line through v. Write it as c v, then require the remainder u-cv to have zero dot product with v. Solving $u\cdot v-c(v\cdot v)=0$ gives the coefficient c. This derivation explains why the denominator uses the target's squared magnitude.

The target v must be nonzero. The source u may be zero, in which case its projection onto a nonzero target is zero. A negative coefficient produces a projection opposite the target's direction. That is a valid projection; it is not a negative vector length.

sections.heading: Scalar component and vector projection answer different questions
paragraphs: The signed scalar component is u dotted with the unit vector along v. It tells how much of u points along that direction, retaining a sign. Multiply that scalar by the unit vector to obtain the vector projection. The projection's magnitude is the absolute value of the scalar component.

After calculating, check that the projection is parallel to v and the remainder is perpendicular to v. You can also check that the squared magnitude of u equals the sum of the squared magnitudes of the perpendicular pieces. These checks expose a swapped target or an incorrect denominator.

sections.heading: Use units and the supplied physical model
paragraphs: For a constant force F acting through displacement d, the supplied model W=F·d gives work by that force. Only the force component along the displacement contributes. A force opposing the displacement gives negative work; a perpendicular force gives zero work in this constant-force calculation.

Work has units N m, conventionally written joules J. The scalar result does not describe all other forces or an entire energy budget. For varying forces, the complete course develops a work integral. Here, keep the model, signs, and units explicit rather than extending the formula beyond its assumptions.
